newsitem.title: USA: Georgia revenue growth seen slowing to under 5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Georgia revenue growth seen slowing to under 5 pct.

text.p: Georgia tax revenues are projected to grow seven percent for 1996, then slow to less than five percent over the next two years, Georgia State University economist Donald Ratajczak said Tuesday in his quarterly forecast.
Ratajczak said the slowdown in revenue growth is expected because of the state's reduction in sales taxes on food, and the end of Olympics-related activity.
State revenues surged by 11.1 percent in the four months that began July 1, but have already slowed to just over 4 percent for October.
Georgia employment is expected to grow by 85,400 in 1997 and 77,600 in 1998, Ratajczak projected. In Atlanta, employement is expected to expand by 50,500 in 1997 and 45,500 in 1998.

Olympic venues, including Atlanta, Athens, Columbus and Savannah, have shown the fastest employment gains since last September. While that growth is slowing, none are expected to slip into recession in the next two years, Ratajczak said.

A modest reduction in housing activity is expected to be offset partly by rising commercial construction. Apparel and paper employment will continue to decline into 1998, but the carpet industry, poultry production and processing, and transportation services should see strong employment gains in the next two years, Ratajczak projected.
Gross state product has increased five percent in 1996 but will slow to 2.5 percent next year and three percent in 1998.
Personal income gains should slow from 7.8 percent in 1995 to seven percent in 1996, 6.4 percent in 1997, and 6.1 percent in 1998.

Farm income should remain strong in the next two years, but the favorable grain and cotton prices that propelled farm income over $3 billion in the first quarter of this year will decline in the next two years, the outlook said.
